property_documents.document:
One possible explanation was that the changes happened accidentally in a region with long growing season and then were introduced to the Sea Islands. In the 1960s and 1970s, S. G. Stephens performed an experiment where he hybridized a G. barbadense with short coarse fibers and long growing season with a wild form of G. hirsutum that had the same short fiber and long growing season, but the fibers were fine. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It seemed reasonable the resulting plant produced fine fibers, but was surprised to find it also had long fiber and short growing season.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He then demonstrated this could be rather easily back-hybridized (see introgression) to form a cotton that retained these desirable characteristics, yet was almost entirely G. barbadense.<</Q_RELEVANT>> He  argued that such an event could have happened accidentally in the 18th century, resulting in the long, fine fiber G. barbadense of today. <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, since this event could not have happened in the Sea Islands, it is not sufficient to explain the Sea Islands' distinctive product.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Sea island never fully recovered from the disruptions of the U.S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Civil War.[2]: 136  In the early 20th century, the boll weevil caused tremendous damage in the traditional cotton-growing regions of the United States.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Sea Island cultivars were particularly susceptible. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Also, wet conditions on the islands moderated soil temperatures, further favoring the insect.[2]: 291–292  Production of Sea Island on a commercial scale ended in 1920.[2]: 332<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Some growers have established trademarks for yarn or finished items made of G. barbadense fiber.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Caribbean producers banded together in 1933 to form the West Indian Sea Island Cotton Association.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The organization allows makers of yarn and finished goods to use the “WISICA” trademark, provided the items are made from Sea Island of the Caribbean cotton and meet certain quality requirements. [18][21] Likewise, a group of southwestern United States growers established the trademark Supima for products made of American Pima fiber.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Most G. barbadense production comes from cultivars that produce particularly long fiber, and most of that is made into clothing.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Fine (thin) yarn requires long fiber. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In turn, this thin yarn is required for intermediate products like lace and high thread-count cloth.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The long-fiber cultivars also tend to have particularly strong fibers, making them useful for various industrial products.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Historically, G. barbadense has been used for the cords of automobile tires and cloth for aircraft wings.[2]: 85  It is also used for sewing machine thread.[2]: 277<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The native range of this species is Colombia to Peru.[1] It is now cultivated around the world, including China, Egypt, Sudan, India, Australia, Peru, Israel, the southwestern United States, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It accounts for about a fifth of the world's cotton production.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>G. barbadense is now cultivated around the world, including China, Egypt, Sudan, India, Australia, Peru, Israel, the southwestern United States, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.[2]: 73–74  The species accounts for about 5% of the world's cotton production.[2]: 88<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>What was called Sea Island cotton was cultivated on the Sea Islands, along the coasts of South Carolina and Georgia, especially by the late 18th century.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Sea Island cotton commanded the highest price of all the cottons because of its long staple (1.5 to 2.5 inches, 38 to 64 mm) and silky texture; it was used for the finest cotton counts and often mixed with silk.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Although planters tried to grow it on the uplands of Georgia, the quality was inferior,[11] and it was too expensive to process. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The invention of the cotton gin by the end of the 18th century utterly changed the production of cotton as a commodity crop.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It made processing of short-staple cotton profitable.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This cotton, known as upland cotton (Gossypium hirsutum), could be grown successfully in the interior uplands.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Short-staple cotton became the prime commodity crop of the developing Deep South, and King Cotton was the basis of southern wealth in the antebellum years.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This cotton in the early 21st century represents about 95% of U.S. production.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

G. barbadense has been grown in the West Indies, and more broadly in the Caribbean region on a small scale since antiquity. It became one of the region's major crops in the 18th century. <<Q_RELEVANT>>This was the traditional form of the species, as varieties with long fibers had not yet been developed.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, Caribbean producers all but abandoned cotton production in the nineteenth century, when sugar cane became more lucrative.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Then, the market for sugar cane declined, leading Caribbean growers to seek another crop. Commercial quantities of long-fiber G. barbasense seeds first came to the Caribbean in 1902.[2]: 84  From this developed the “Sea Island of the Caribbean” market class.[18]

property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The production methods have not significantly changed since ancient times.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Through selective breeding of the Papaver somniferum plant, the content of the phenanthrene alkaloids morphine, codeine, and to a lesser extent thebaine has been greatly increased.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In modern times, much of the thebaine, which often serves as the raw material for the synthesis for oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, and other semisynthetic opiates, originates from extracting Papaver orientale or Papaver bracteatum. In preparation for the Second World War, the U.S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Army contracted farmers in the State of Sinaloa, Mexico, to grow opium crops.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This was to provide morphine (the gold standard of analgesia) for injured soldiers. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Modern opium production, once widely prohibited, still involves large-scale cultivation—especially in Afghanistan—where it is harvested by scoring poppy pods to collect latex used for both illicit drugs and legal medicines, with recent Taliban-led reductions cutting cultivation in Afghanistan by over 95%.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Eventually, laudanum became readily available and extensively used by the 18th century in Europe, especially England.[38] Compared to other chemicals available to 18th century regular physicians, opium was a benign alternative to arsenic, mercury, or emetics, and it was remarkably successful in alleviating a wide range of ailments.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Due to the constipation often produced by the consumption of opium, it was one of the most effective treatments for cholera, dysentery, and diarrhea.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As a cough suppressant, opium was used to treat bronchitis, tuberculosis, and other respiratory illnesses.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Opium was additionally prescribed for rheumatism and insomnia.[39] Medical textbooks even recommended its use by people in good health, to "optimize the internal equilibrium of the human body".[24]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Seed capsules can be dried and used for decorations, but they also contain morphine, codeine, and other alkaloids.<</Q_RELEVANT>> These pods can be boiled in water to produce a bitter tea that induces a long-lasting intoxication. <<Q_RELEVANT>>If allowed to mature, poppy pods (poppy straw) can be crushed and used to produce lower quantities of morphinans.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In poppies subjected to mutagenesis and selection on a mass scale, researchers have been able to use poppy straw to obtain large quantities of oripavine, a precursor to opioids and antagonists such as naltrexone.[124] Although millennia older, the production of poppy head decoctions can be seen as a quick-and-dirty variant of the Kábáy poppy straw process, which since its publication in 1930 has become the major method of obtaining licit opium alkaloids worldwide, as discussed in Morphine.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>When grown for opium production, the skin of the ripening pods of these poppies is scored by a sharp blade at a time carefully chosen so that rain, wind, and dew cannot spoil the exudation of white, milky latex, usually in the afternoon.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Incisions are made while the pods are still raw, with no more than a slight yellow tint, and must be shallow to avoid penetrating hollow inner chambers or loculi while cutting into the lactiferous vessels. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the Indian Subcontinent, Afghanistan, Central Asia and Iran, the special tool used to make the incisions is called a nushtar or "nishtar" (from Persian, meaning a lancet) and carries three or four blades three millimeters apart, which are scored upward along the pod.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Incisions are made three or four times at intervals of two to three days, and each time the "poppy tears", which dry to a sticky brown resin, are collected the following morning. <<Q_RELEVANT>>One acre harvested in this way can produce three to five kilograms of raw opium.[129] In the Soviet Union, pods were typically scored horizontally, and opium was collected three times, or else one or two collections were followed by isolation of opiates from the ripe capsules.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Oil poppies, an alternative strain of P. somniferum, were also used for production of opiates from their capsules and stems.[130] A traditional Chinese method of harvesting opium latex involved cutting off the heads and piercing them with a coarse needle then collecting the dried opium 24 to 48 hours later.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>A phylogenetic or cladistic species is "the smallest aggregation of populations (sexual) or lineages (asexual) diagnosable by a unique combination of character states in comparable individuals (semaphoronts)".[35] The empirical basis – observed character states – provides the evidence to support hypotheses about evolutionarily divergent lineages that have maintained their hereditary integrity through time and space.[36][37][38][39] Molecular markers may be used to determine diagnostic genetic differences in the nuclear or mitochondrial DNA of various species.[40][35][41] For example, in a study done on fungi, studying the nucleotide characters using cladistic species produced the most accurate results in recognising the numerous fungi species of all the concepts studied.[41][42] Versions of the phylogenetic species concept that emphasise monophyly or diagnosability[43] may lead to splitting of existing species, for example in Bovidae, by recognising old subspecies as species, despite the fact that there are no reproductive barriers, and populations may intergrade morphologically.[44] Others have called this approach taxonomic inflation, diluting the species concept and making taxonomy unstable.[45] Yet others defend this approach, considering "taxonomic inflation" pejorative and labelling the opposing view as "taxonomic conservatism"; claiming it is politically expedient to split species and recognise smaller populations at the species level, because this means they can more easily be included as endangered in the IUCN red list and can attract conservation legislation and funding.[46]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>A typological species is a group of organisms in which individuals conform to certain fixed properties (a type, which may be defined by a chosen 'nominal species'), so that even pre-literate people often recognise the same taxon as do modern taxonomists.[10][11] Modern-day field guides and identification websites such as iNaturalist use this concept.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The clusters of variations or phenotypes within specimens (such as longer or shorter tails) would differentiate the species.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This method was used as a "classical" method of determining species, such as with Linnaeus, early in evolutionary theory.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, different phenotypes are not necessarily different species (e.g. a four-winged Drosophila born to a two-winged mother is not a different species).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Species named in this manner are called morphospecies.[12][13]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>While the definitions given above may seem adequate at first glance, when looked at more closely they represent problematic species concepts.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>For example, the boundaries between closely related species become unclear with hybridisation, in a species complex of hundreds of similar microspecies, and in a ring species.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Also, among organisms that reproduce only asexually, the concept of a reproductive species breaks down, and each clonal lineage is potentially a microspecies.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Although none of these are entirely satisfactory definitions, and while the concept of species may not be a perfect model of life, it is still a useful tool to scientists and conservationists for studying life on Earth, regardless of the theoretical difficulties.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>If species were fixed and distinct from one another, there would be no problem, but evolutionary processes cause species to change.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This obliges taxonomists to decide, for example, when enough change has occurred to declare that a fossil lineage should be divided into multiple chronospecies, or when populations have diverged to have enough distinct character states to be described as cladistic species.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The evolutionary process by which biological populations of sexually-reproducing organisms evolve to become distinct or reproductively isolated as species is called speciation.[138][139] Charles Darwin was the first to describe the role of natural selection in speciation in his 1859 book The Origin of Species.[140] Speciation depends on a measure of reproductive isolation, a reduced gene flow.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This occurs most easily in allopatric speciation, where populations are separated geographically and can diverge gradually as mutations accumulate. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Reproductive isolation is threatened by hybridisation, but this can be selected against once a pair of populations have incompatible alleles of the same gene, as described in the Bateson–Dobzhansky–Muller model.[135] A different mechanism, phyletic speciation, involves one lineage gradually changing over time into a new and distinct form (a chronospecies), without increasing the number of resultant species.[141]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

With the advent of the Industrial Revolution, Britain surged ahead of its European rivals. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Demand for Indian commodities was boosted by the need to sustain troops and the economy during the war, and by the increased availability of raw materials and efficient methods of production.<</Q_RELEVANT>> As home to the revolution, Britain experienced higher standards of living. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its ever-growing cycle of prosperity, demand and production had a profound influence on overseas trade.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The company became the single largest player in the British global market. In 1801 Henry Dundas reported to the House of Commons that

In the 18th Century, the primary source of the Company's profits in Bengal became taxation in conquered and controlled provinces, as the factories became fortresses and administrative hubs for networks of tax collectors that expanded into enormous cities. <<A_RELEVANT>>The Mughal Empire was the richest in the world in 1700, and the East India Company tried to strip it bare for a century thereafter.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Dalrymple calls it "the single largest transfer of wealth until the Nazis."[45] What was in the 17th century the production capital of the world for textiles was forced to become a market for British-made textiles.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Statues, jewels, and various other valuables were moved from the palaces of Bengal to the townhouses of the English countryside. Bengal in particular suffered the worst of Company tax farming, highlighted by the Great Bengal famine of 1770.[45]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>When the news arrived in England it caused an outcry.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>To appease Aurangzeb, the East India Company promised to pay all financial reparations, while Parliament declared the pirates hostis humani generis ("the enemy of humanity").[citation needed] In mid-1696 the government issued a £500 bounty on Every's head and offered a free pardon to any informer who disclosed his whereabouts.<</A_RELEVANT>> The first worldwide manhunt in recorded history was underway.[61]: 144

In September the company took out a loan from the Bank of England, to be repaid from the sale of goods later that month. But with buyers scarce, most of the sale had to be postponed, and when the loan fell due, the company's coffers were empty. <<Q_RELEVANT>>On October 29 the bank refused to renew the loan.<</Q_RELEVANT>> That decision set in motion a chain of events that made the American Revolution inevitable. <<A_RELEVANT>>The East India Company had eighteen million pounds of tea sitting in British warehouses.<</A_RELEVANT>> A huge amount of tea as assets which were lying unsold. Selling it in a hurry would do wonders for its finances.[89]

<<A_RELEVANT>>The East India Company had also been granted competitive advantages over colonial American tea importers to sell tea from its colonies in Asia in American colonies.<</A_RELEVANT>> This led to the Boston Tea Party of 1773 in which protesters boarded British ships and threw the tea overboard. <<Q_RELEVANT>>When protesters successfully prevented the unloading of tea in three other colonies and in Boston, Governor Thomas Hutchinson of the Province of Massachusetts Bay refused to allow the tea to be returned to Britain.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This was one of the incidents which led to the American Revolution and independence of the American colonies.[92]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Originally chartered as the "Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East-Indies,"[6][7] the company rose to account for half of the world's trade during the mid-1700s and early 1800s,[8] particularly in basic commodities including cotton, silk, indigo dye, sugar, salt, spices, saltpetre, tea, gemstones, and later opium.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The company also initiated the beginnings of the British Raj in the Indian subcontinent.[8][9]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The biggest prize that galvanised English trade was the seizure of a large Portuguese carrack, the Madre de Deus, by Walter Raleigh and the Earl of Cumberland at the Battle of Flores on 13 August 1592.[20] When she was brought in to Dartmouth she was the largest vessel ever seen in England and she carried chests of jewels, pearls, gold, silver coins, ambergris, cloth, tapestries, pepper, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, benjamin (a highly aromatic balsamic resin used for perfumes and medicines), red dye, cochineal and ebony.[21] Equally valuable was the ship's rutter (mariner's handbook) containing vital information on the China, India, and Japan trade routes.[20]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Sericulture
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Sericulture, or silk farming, is the cultivation of silkworms to produce silk.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Although there are several commercial species of silkworms, the caterpillar of the domestic silkmoth is the most widely used and intensively studied silkworm.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This species of silkmoth is no longer found in the wild as they have been modified through selective breeding, rendering most flightless and without defense against predators.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Silk is believed to have first been produced in China as early as the Neolithic period.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Today, China and India are the two main producers, with more than 60% of the world's annual production.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>According to Confucian text[which?], the discovery of silk production dates to about 2700 BCE, although archaeological records point to silk cultivation as early as the Yangshao period (5000–3000 BCE).[1] In 1977, a piece of ceramic created 5400–5500 years ago and designed to look like a silkworm was discovered in Nancun, Hebei, providing the earliest known evidence of sericulture.[2] Also, by careful analysis of archaeological silk fibre found on Indus Civilization sites dating back to 2450–2000 BCE, it is believed that silk was being used over a wide region of South Asia.[3][4] By about the first half of the 1st century CE, it had reached ancient Khotan,[5] by a series of interactions along the Silk Road.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>By 140 CE, the practice had been established in India.[6] In the 6th century CE, the smuggling of silkworm eggs into the Byzantine Empire led to its establishment in the Mediterranean, remaining a monopoly in the Byzantine Empire for centuries (Byzantine silk).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1147, during the Second Crusade, Roger II of Sicily (1095–1154) attacked Corinth and Thebes, two important centres of Byzantine silk production, capturing the weavers and their equipment and establishing his own silkworks in Palermo and Calabria,[7] eventually spreading the industry to Western Europe.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The cocoons of Tussar silkworms, which are found in open woodlands, are used to produce wild silk, also known as Tussar silk.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Compared to conventional silk, their cocoons are typically picked after the moths have emerged, making it a more ethical option.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Because wild silkworms consume a variety of plants, their fabric is less uniform but more robust.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Wild silk production, especially that of Tussar silk, typically involves fewer chemical treatments than conventional silk because it is often processed without degumming or bleaching, processes commonly used in mulberry silk production.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The pupae are still inside the cocoons when they are harvested by certain enterprises that employ "wild silk", though.[11]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The conventional method of silk production results in ~8 kg of wet silkworm pupae and ~2 kg of dry pupae per kilogram of raw silk.[16] This byproduct has historically been consumed by people in silk-producing areas.[16][17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The most popular substitute for traditional silk is peace silk, also known as ahimsa silk.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The primary factor that makes this form of silk more ethical is that moths are permitted to emerge from their cocoons and fly away prior to boiling.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It denotes that no pupa is ever cooked alive during manufacture. <<QA_RELEVANT>>However, domesticated silkworms used to make silk have undergone thousands of years of selective breeding and are not "manufactured" to emerge from their cocoons.<</QA_RELEVANT>> They are unable to defend themselves against predators since they cannot fly or see clearly. They typically die soon after emerging from their cocoons as a result.[10]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Mahatma Gandhi was critical of silk production based on the Ahimsa philosophy "not to hurt any living thing".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He also promoted "Ahimsa silk", made without boiling the pupa to procure the silk and wild silk made from the cocoons of wild and semiwild silkmoths.[13][14][failed verification] The Human League also criticised sericulture in their early single "Being Boiled".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The organisation PETA has also campaigned against silk.[15]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The silkworms are fed with mulberry leaves, and after the fourth moult, they climb a twig placed near them and spin their silken cocoons.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The silk is a continuous filament comprising fibroin protein, secreted from two salivary glands in the head of each worm, and a gum called sericin, which cements the filaments.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The sericin is removed by placing the cocoons in hot water, which frees the silk filaments and readies them for reeling.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This is known as the degumming process.[8] The immersion in hot water also kills the silkmoth pupa.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Single filaments are combined to form thread, in a process called "throwing", which is drawn under tension through several guides and wound onto reels. <<Q_RELEVANT>>This process of throwing produces various yarns depending on the amount and direction of the twisting.[9] The threads may be plied to form yarn (short staple lengths are spun; see silk noil).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After drying, the raw silk is packed according to quality.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The silkworms and mulberry leaves are placed on trays.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Twig frames for the silkworms are prepared.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The cocoons are boiled and the silk is wound on spools.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: This chartered corporation’s archives are held by the International Institute of Social History, an organization whose work focuses on the history of communism, and its child company’s records are also stored at the Nationaal Archief. The corporation owned a colonial capital located on the Houtman Abrolhos archipelago. Based on these clues, identify the corporation and state: in which century (as an ordinal number) was this organization founded?

entity_document.title: Dutch East India Company
entity_document.text:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The VOC's operations (trading posts and colonies) produced not only warehouses packed with spices, coffee, tea, textiles, porcelain and silk, but also shiploads of documents.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Data on political, economic, cultural, religious, and social conditions spread over an enormous area circulated between the VOC establishments, the administrative centre of the trade in Batavia (modern-day Jakarta), and the board of directors (the Heeren XVII [nl]/Gentlemen Seventeen) in the Dutch Republic.[101] Twenty-five million pages of VOC records survive, held in Jakarta; Colombo, Sri Lanka; Chennai, India; Cape Town, South Africa; and The Hague, the Netherlands.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2003, UNESCO added this collection of records to its Memory of the World international register.[102]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

By the time the settlement was established at the Cape in 1652, the VOC already had a long experience of practicing slavery in the East Indies. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Jan van Riebeeck concluded within two months of the establishment of the Cape settlement that slave labor would be needed for the hardest and dirtiest work.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Initially, the VOC considered enslaving men from the indigenous Khoikhoi population, but the idea was rejected on the grounds that such a policy would be both costly and dangerous. Most Khoikhoi had chosen not to labor for the Dutch because of low wages and harsh conditions. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the beginning, the settlers traded with the Khoikhoi, but the harsh working conditions and low wages imposed by the Dutch led to a series of wars.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The European population remained under 200 during the settlement's first five years, and war against neighbors numbering more than 20,000 would have been foolhardy. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Moreover, the Dutch feared that Khoikhoi people, if enslaved, could always escape into the local community, whereas foreigners would find it much more difficult to escape and survive or avoid recapture.[99]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The attempt to continue as before as a low volume-high profit business enterprise with its core business in the spice trade had therefore failed.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The company had however already (reluctantly) followed the example of its European competitors in diversifying into other Asian commodities, like tea, coffee, cotton, textiles, and sugar. <<Q_RELEVANT>>These commodities provided a lower profit margin and therefore required a larger sales volume to generate the same amount of revenue.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This structural change in the commodity composition of the VOC's trade started in the early 1680s, after the temporary collapse of the EIC around 1683 offered an excellent opportunity to enter these markets.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The actual cause for the change lies, however, in two structural features of this new era.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Statistically, the VOC eclipsed all of its rivals in the Asian trade.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Between 1602 and 1796, the VOC sent nearly a million Europeans to work in the Asia trade on 4,785 ships, and netted for their efforts more than 2.5 million tons of Asian trade goods and slaves.<</Q_RELEVANT>> By contrast, the rest of Europe combined sent 882,412 people from 1500 to 1795. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The fleet of the English, later British East India Company, the VOC's nearest competitor, was a distant second to its total traffic, with 2,690 ships and one-fifth the tonnage of goods carried by the VOC.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The VOC enjoyed huge profits from its spice monopoly through most of the 17th century.[12]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In Dutch, the name of the company was the Vereenigde Nederlandsche Geoctroyeerde Oostindische Compagnie, abbreviated as the VOC, literally the 'United Dutch Chartered East India Company' (the United East India Company).[15] The company's monogram logo consisted of a large capital 'V' with an O on the left and a C on the right half and was possibly the first globally recognised corporate logo.[16] It appeared on corporate items, such as flags, cannons, and coins.[16][17]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1580, the Portuguese crown was united in a personal union with the Spanish crown, known as the Iberian Union, with which the Dutch Republic was at war.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The Portuguese Empire thus became an appropriate target for Dutch military incursions. <<Q_RELEVANT>>These factors motivated Dutch merchants to enter the intercontinental spice trade themselves.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Further, a number of Dutch merchants and explorers, such as Jan Huyghen van Linschoten and Cornelis de Houtman, obtained firsthand knowledge of the "secret" Portuguese trade routes and practices, providing further opportunity for the Dutch to enter the trade.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: International Institute of Social History
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The International Institute of Social History (IISH/IISG) is one of the largest archives of labor and social history in the world.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Located in Amsterdam, its one million volumes and 5,445 archival collections include the papers of major figures and institutions in radical leftist thought.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The IISH was founded in 1935 by Nicolaas Posthumus as an independent scientific institute. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is part of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>IISG hosts part of the IHLIA LGBT Heritage collection (LGBT Archives).[9]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Jaap Kloosterman, Jan Lucassen et al.: 'Working for Labour.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Three quarters of a century of collecting at the IISH'. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In: Rebels with a Cause.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Amsterdam, Aksant, 2010. ISBN 9789052603896

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The International Institute of Social History specializes in international labor and social history, including that of the Netherlands.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As of 2000, it holds one million volumes, 80,000 audiovisual items, 2,400 serials, three million digital files, and 30,000 linear feet of manuscripts across 5,445 collections.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Among the latter are institutional collections from Amnesty International, Confederación Nacional del Trabajo and Federación Anarquista Ibérica, the European Trade Union Confederation, Freedom Press, Greenpeace International, the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, Russian Socialist Revolutionary Party, Socialist International, and the personal papers of Emma Goldman, Karl Marx, Max Nettlau, Lev Trotsky, Karl Kautsky, Ernest Mandel, and Sylvia Pankhurst.[1] The institute is the foremost repository of anarchist documents in the world.[2][3]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Nicolaas Posthumus, a socialist and first chair appointment in economic history in the Netherlands,[1] founded the International Institute of Social History in 1935.[4] To examine how labour relations develop over time, IISG collected archives from all over the world.<</Q_RELEVANT>> During the first years Posthumus succeeded in obtaining many papers from anarchists (Bakunin manuscripts), other socialist and social democratic and Marxist movements from Germany and Russia.[5]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Before the Germans invaded the Netherlands in May 1940, Posthumus was able to move the most valuable archives to London.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>During the war, most remaining IISG archives were transported to Nazi Germany between June 1942 and September 1944 by agents of the Reichsleiter Rosenberg Taskforce led by Eberhard Kautter.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>They were not destroyed, but stored for eventual inclusion in the Advanced School of the NSDAP.[6] Most of the papers were rediscovered in Hannover in 1946, and some other parts were later found in archives in Moscow in 1991, and returned to Amsterdam.[7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Blok, Aad; Lucassen, Jan; Sanders, Huub, eds. (2014). <<Q_RELEVANT>>A Usable Collection: Essays in Honour of Jaap Kloosterman on Collecting Social History.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press. doi:10.26530/OAPEN_496214. ISBN 978-90-8964-688-0.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1989 the International Institute of Social History moved to new premises: an old warehouse at the Cruquiusweg in the eastern part of Amsterdam.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This building also housed the Press Museum but in 2017 that museum became a part of the Dutch Institute for Image and Sound (Nederlands Instituut voor Beeld en Geluid) in Hilversum.[8]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Nationaal Archief (NA) is the national archives of the Netherlands, located in The Hague.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It houses collections for the central government, the province of South Holland, and the former County of Holland.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>There is also material from private institutions and individuals with an association to the Dutch government or the political or social history of the Netherlands.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The Nationaal Archief holds the Archives of the Dutch East India Company from 1602 to 1811, which were, along with related records held by South Africa, India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia, inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World International Register in 2003 in recognition of their historical value.[1]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Houtman Abrolhos
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Other shipwrecks, notably Zeewijk (also spelled Zeewyk), have also become the subject of books and other works.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Other cultural references to the Houtman Abrolhos are rare.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>By far the best known book on it is Malcolm Uren's Sailormen's ghosts: The Abrolhos islands in three hundred years of romance, history, and adventure.[citation needed] First published in 1940, this book saw numerous editions published in the 1940s, and was even republished in 1980 as a "West Australian classic".[citation needed] In it, Uren tells both the history of the islands and the story of his own visit to the islands.[85]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In marine terms, the Houtman Abrolhos is located within the Southwest Shelf Transition, an Integrated Marine and Coastal Regionalisation of Australia (IMCRA) biotone that takes in the continental shelf from Perth to Geraldton.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This province is defined as the area of shelf where tropical waters intergrade into temperate, thus supporting both tropical and temperate biota.[39][40] In addition, this area contains the highest concentration of west coast endemics.[41]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The vascular flora of the Houtman Abrolhos has been thoroughly surveyed, and species lists have been published for 119 islands.<</Q_RELEVANT>> As of 2001, these lists totalled 239 species from 68 families. <<Q_RELEVANT>>A further six species have been collected in the Houtman Abrolhos, but cannot be allocated to islands because insufficient location information was recorded.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>There have also been collections of mosses, liverworts and lichens, but no information has been published on these non-vascular groups.[42]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The coral reef community at the Houtman Abrolhos is unusual in having tropical coral growing alongside and in direct competition with, temperate seaweed.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As a result of this competition for light, space and nutrients, coral at the Houtman Abrolhos tends to grow more slowly and die younger than is usual.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Reef production is to a large extent due to the production of carbon by coralline algae rather than by coral.[72]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Scallop fishers mainly operate east of the Houtman Abrolhos and between the island groups, in waters deeper than 30 metres (98 ft).<</Q_RELEVANT>> Activity is targeted at sheltered areas of bare sand, where scallops tend to settle. Catches vary greatly from year to year; from 2001 to 2003, for example, the total annual catch totalled 1,182, 195 and 5,840 tonnes or 2.61, 0.43 and 12.87 million pounds (whole weight) respectively. <<Q_RELEVANT>>This variability is apparently related to the strength of the Leeuwin Current, as strong current is correlated with low scallop recruitment.[81]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Mean sea levels at Geraldton show seasonal fluctuations, being higher in winter when the Leeuwin Current is at its peak. <<Q_RELEVANT>>There are also variations from year to year, which are strongly associated with the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Apparently, ENSO events induce a weaker Leeuwin Current, which results in lower sea levels.[34]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The islands have a Mediterranean climate (semi-arid climate, or BSh, under Köppen climate classification) with warm dry summers and cooler, wet winters.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Mean temperatures range from 9.3 to 19.5 °C (48.7 to 67.1 °F) in July, and from 19.1 to 32.4 °C (66.4 to 90.3 °F) in February. These temperatures have a substantially smaller range than on the mainland: the summer temperature is typically a degree cooler, while winter temperatures are a good deal warmer. This is due to the influence of the ocean, and to the Leeuwin Current.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Three classes of storm have been identified for the region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Brief squalls may occur between December and April. A tropical cyclone occurs in the area about once in three years, between January and April; these may generate extremely high wind speeds that are potentially destructive. <<Q_RELEVANT>>During winter, extra-tropical cyclones sometimes pass south of Geraldton, generating winter gales with gusts of up to 35 metres per second, the wind direction from the northwest initially, then gradually moving around to southerly.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The story has spawned a massive body of literature, both fiction and non-fiction,[28] as well as numerous works in other media.[citation needed][84]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The islands are an unincorporated area with no municipal government, subject to direct administration of the Government of Western Australia.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In July 2019, the Houtman Abrolhos was declared a national park by the state government.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The word abrolho is Portuguese, making the Houtman Abrolhos one of only two Australian places with a Portuguese name, the other being Pedra Branca in Tasmania.[19] The noun abrolhos means 'thorn', and originally designated the spiny fruit of the bindii plant (Tribulus terrestris).<</Q_RELEVANT>> Etymologically it is a contraction of the Portuguese expression abre os olhos (transl. open your eyes; that is, to protect yourself). As a technical term this phytonym was later applied to caltrops (chevaux de frise), i.e. "spiked obstructions", and Portuguese sailors used the word to refer to offshore reefs.

question: The conflict that erupted after the Dred Scott decision, featured John Brown’s raid on Harpers Ferry, and concluded with the Compromise of 1877 during the Reconstruction Era is the focus of this inquiry. How many years separate the beginning of this war from the start of the next calendar century?

entity_document.title: American Civil War
entity_document.text:
Kentucky did not secede but declared itself neutral. <<Q_RELEVANT>>When Confederate forces entered in September 1861, its neutrality ended and the state reaffirmed its Union status while maintaining slavery.<</Q_RELEVANT>> During an invasion by Confederate forces in 1861, Confederate sympathizers and delegates from 68 Kentucky counties organized the secession Russellville Convention, formed the shadow Confederate Government of Kentucky, inaugurated a governor, and Kentucky was admitted into the Confederacy on December 10, 1861. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its jurisdiction extended only as far as Confederate battle lines in the Commonwealth, which at its greatest extent was over half the state, and it went into exile after October 1862.[72]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

By the end of the war, much of the South's infrastructure had been destroyed. The Confederacy collapsed, slavery was abolished, and four million enslaved black people were freed. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The war-torn nation then entered the Reconstruction era in an attempt to rebuild the country, bring the former Confederate states back into the United States, and grant civil rights to freed slaves.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The war is one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It remains the subject of cultural and historiographical debate.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Of continuing interest is the myth of the Lost Cause of the Confederacy. The war was among the first to use industrial warfare. Railroads, the electrical telegraph, steamships, the ironclad warship, and mass-produced weapons were widely used. The war left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, along with an undetermined number of civilian deaths, making it the deadliest in American history.[g] The technology and brutality of the Civil War foreshadowed the coming world wars.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In December 1860, the Crittenden Compromise was proposed to re-establish the Missouri Compromise line, by constitutionally banning slavery in territories to the north of it, while permitting it to the south.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Compromise would likely have prevented secession, but Lincoln and the Republicans rejected it.[42] Lincoln stated that any compromise that would extend slavery would bring down the Union.[43] A February peace conference met in Washington, proposing a solution similar to the Compromise; it was rejected by Congress.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The Republicans proposed the Corwin Amendment, an alternative, not to interfere with slavery where it existed, but the South regarded it as insufficient. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The remaining eight slave states rejected pleas to join the Confederacy, following a no-vote in Virginia's First Secessionist Convention on April 4.[44]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The American Civil War began on April 12, 1861, when Confederate forces opened fire on the Union-held Fort Sumter.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Fort Sumter is located in the harbor of Charleston, South Carolina.[50] Its status had been contentious for months.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Outgoing president Buchanan had dithered in reinforcing its garrison, commanded by Major Robert Anderson. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Anderson took matters into his own hands and on December 26, 1860, under the cover of darkness, sailed the garrison from the poorly placed Fort Moultrie to the stalwart island Fort Sumter.[51] Anderson's actions catapulted him to hero status in the North.<</Q_RELEVANT>> An attempt to resupply the fort on January 9, 1861, failed and nearly started the war then, but an informal truce held.[52] On March 5, Lincoln was informed the fort was low on supplies.[53]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>After the Emancipation Proclamation authorized freed slaves to "be received into the armed service of the United States", former slaves who escaped from plantations or were liberated by the Union Army were recruited into the United States Colored Troops regiments of the Union Army, as were black men who had not been slaves.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The US Colored Troops made up 10 percent of the Union death toll—15 percent of Union deaths from disease and less than 3 percent of those killed in battle.[5] Losses among African Americans were high. In the last year and a half and from all reported casualties, approximately 20 percent of all African Americans enrolled in the military died during the war. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Their mortality rate was significantly higher than white soldiers.<</Q_RELEVANT>> While 15 percent of US Volunteers and just 9 percent of white Regular Army troops died, 21 percent of US Colored Troops died.[272]: 16

Inflicting an ever-tightening naval blockade of Confederate ports, the Union marshaled resources and manpower to attack the Confederacy from all directions. This led to the fall of Atlanta in 1864 to Union general William Tecumseh Sherman, followed by his March to the Sea, which culminated in his taking Savannah. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The last significant battles raged around the ten-month Siege of Petersburg, gateway to the Confederate capital of Richmond.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Confederates abandoned Richmond, and on April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered to Grant following the Battle of Appomattox Court House, setting in motion the end of the war.[f] Lincoln lived to see this victory but was shot by an assassin on April 14, dying the next day.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Supreme Court of the United States
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Taney Court (1836–1864) made several important rulings, such as Sheldon v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Sill, which held that while Congress may not limit the subjects the Supreme Court may hear, it may limit the jurisdiction of the lower federal courts to prevent them from hearing cases dealing with certain subjects.[33] Nevertheless, it is primarily remembered for its ruling in Dred Scott v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Sandford,[34] which helped precipitate the American Civil War.[35] In the Reconstruction era, the Chase, Waite, and Fuller Courts (1864–1910) interpreted the new Civil War amendments to the Constitution[28] and developed the doctrine of substantive due process (Lochner v.<</QA_RELEVANT>> New York;[36] Adair v. <<Q_RELEVANT>>United States).[37] The size of the court was last changed in 1869, when it was set at nine.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Court also relies on and cites amicus briefs, law review articles, and other written works for their decisions.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>While law review article use has increased slightly with one article cited per decision on average,[215] the use of amicus briefs has increased significantly.[216] The use of amicus briefs has received criticism, including the ability of authors to discuss topics outside their expertise (unlike in lower courts),[216] with documented examples of falsehoods in written opinions, often supplied to the justices by amicus briefs from groups advocating a particular outcome.[217] The lack of funding transparency and the lack of a requirement to submit them earlier in the process also make it more difficult to fact-check and understand the credibility of amicus briefs.[216]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Supreme Court relies on the record assembled by lower courts for the facts of a case and deals solely with the question of how the law applies to the facts presented.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>There are however situations where the court has original jurisdiction, such as when two states have a dispute against each other, or when there is a dispute between the United States and a state.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In such instances, a case is filed with the Supreme Court directly.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Examples of such cases include United States v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Texas, a case to determine whether a parcel of land belonged to the United States or to Texas, and Virginia v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Tennessee, a case turning on whether an incorrectly drawn boundary between two states can be changed by a state court, and whether the setting of the correct boundary requires Congressional approval.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Although it has not happened since 1794 in the case of Georgia v. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Brailsford,[208] parties in an action at law in which the Supreme Court has original jurisdiction may request that a jury determine issues of fact.[209] Georgia v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Brailsford remains the only case in which the court has empaneled a jury, in this case a special jury.[210] Two other original jurisdiction cases involve colonial era borders and rights under navigable waters in New Jersey v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware, and water rights between riparian states upstream of navigable waters in Kansas v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Colorado.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>There are two living retired justices of the Supreme Court of the United States: Anthony Kennedy and Stephen Breyer.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As retired justices, they no longer participate in the work of the Supreme Court, but may be designated for temporary assignments to sit on lower federal courts, usually the United States Courts of Appeals.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Such assignments are formally made by the chief justice, on request of the chief judge of the lower court and with the consent of the retired justice.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The status of a retired justice is analogous to that of a circuit or district court judge who has taken senior status, and eligibility of a Supreme Court justice to assume retired status (rather than simply resign from the bench) is governed by the same age and service criteria.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In addition, the other two branches can restrain the court through other mechanisms.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Congress can increase the number of justices, giving the president power to influence future decisions by appointments (as in Roosevelt's court-packing plan discussed above).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Congress can pass legislation that restricts the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other federal courts over certain topics and cases: this is suggested by language in Section 2 of Article Three, where the appellate jurisdiction is granted "with such Exceptions, and under such Regulations as the Congress shall make." The court sanctioned such congressional action in the Reconstruction Era case Ex parte McCardle (1869), although it rejected Congress' power to dictate how particular cases must be decided in United States v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Klein (1871).[245]

property_documents.title: Compromise of 1877
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>No written evidence of such a deal has ever been found, and its precise details are a matter of historical debate, but  historians agree that the federal government adopted a policy of leniency towards the South to ensure federal authority and Hayes's successful election as president.[1] The existence of an informal agreement to secure Hayes's political authority, known as the Bargain of 1877, was long accepted as a part of American history.[1] Its terms were reviewed by historian C.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Vann Woodward in his 1951 book Reunion and Reaction: The Compromise of 1877 and the End of Reconstruction, which also coined the modern name in an effort to compare the political resolution of the election to the famous Missouri Compromise and Compromise of 1850.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Under the compromise, Democrats controlling the House of Representatives allowed the decision of the Electoral Commission to take effect, securing political legitimacy for Hayes's legal authority as president.[3][clarification needed] The subsequent withdrawal of the last federal troops from the Southern United States effectively ended the Reconstruction Era and forfeited the Republican claims to the state governments in South Carolina, Florida and Louisiana.[4] The outgoing president, Republican Ulysses S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Grant, removed the soldiers from Florida, and as president, Hayes removed the remaining troops from South Carolina and Louisiana.<</Q_RELEVANT>> As soon as the troops left, many white Republicans also left, and the "Redeemer" Democrats, who already dominated other state governments in the South, took control. Some Black Republicans felt betrayed as they lost their political legitimacy in the South that had been defended by the federal military, and by 1905 most African-American people were effectively disenfranchised in every Southern state.[5]

Contemporary accounts of the 1877 crisis lack any discussion of the backroom negotiations. Neither Abram Hewitt's papers nor a 1901 history written by select committee secretary Milton H. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Northrup mentions any sort of deal to secure Hayes's presidency, though Woodward argues that neither man would have been privy to such talks.[10] In his 1913 "inside history" of the crisis, Henry Watterson recounts a White House dinner during the first Grover Cleveland administration, at which four unnamed insiders attempted to outdo each other in revealing the most salacious secret from the 1877 crisis, though Watterson himself concludes "the whole truth... will never be known."[11] Despite the lack of solid contemporary accounts, after the crisis the story of a "Bargain of 1877" had gradually come to plausibly explain how Southern Democrats, though convinced that Tilden was the lawful President, were persuaded to recognize Hayes's authority.[12]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Criticism from other historians has taken various forms, ranging from outright rejection of the compromise theory to criticism of Woodward's emphasis of certain influences or outcomes,[6][7] but critics agree that the event became almost universally accepted in the years after Woodward published Reunion and Reaction.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In the November 1876 United States presidential election, Samuel J.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Tilden received 184 uncontested electoral votes and Rutherford B. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Hayes received 165, with 185 votes necessary for a majority.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Four states (Florida, Louisiana, Oregon, and South Carolina) returned disputed slates of presidential electors with a total of 20 electoral votes at stake. Any of the disputes being resolved in Tilden's favor would secure him the presidency, while Hayes needed all 20 votes to be certified in his favor. To resolve these disputes in the absence of a clear constitutional directive, Congress passed the Electoral Commission Act, which established a 15-member commission of eight Republicans and seven Democrats to review the contested elections.[8]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Some historians, such as Allan Peskin in Was There a Compromise of 1877? (1973), argue that both Hayes's election and the assurances offered to Southern Democrats to prevent a filibuster were not a compromise at all.[17] Though Peskin admits that Woodward's interpretation had become almost universally accepted in the nearly quarter century since he had published it, he argues that three of Woodward's five conditions for compromise were not met, and those which were met were not made for the purpose of securing Hayes's legitimacy.[17] Hayes had already announced prior to the election that he supported the restoration of "home rule", including the withdrawal of federal troops and at the time, it was not unusual nor unexpected for a president, especially one so narrowly elected, to select a cabinet member favored by the other party.[17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.document:
The U.S. president is the head of state, commander-in-chief of the military, and chief executive of the federal government. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The president appoints the members of the Cabinet, subject to Senate approval, and names other officials who administer and enforce federal law and policy through their respective agencies.[247] The president has the ability to veto legislative bills from the U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Congress before they become law. <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, presidential vetoes can be overridden by a two-thirds supermajority vote in both chambers of Congress.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The president also has clemency power for federal crimes and can issue pardons. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Finally, the president has the authority to issue expansive "executive orders" in a number of policy areas, subject to judicial review.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Candidates for president campaign with a vice-presidential running mate. Both candidates are elected together, or defeated together, in a presidential election. Unlike other votes in American politics, this is technically an indirect election in which the winner will be determined by the U.S. Electoral College. There, votes are officially cast by individual electors selected by their state legislature.[248] In practice, however, each of the 50 states chooses a group of presidential electors who are required by state law to confirm the winner of their state's popular vote. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Each state is allocated two electors plus one additional elector for every congressional district in the state, which in effect combines to equal the number of elected officials that state sends to Congress.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The District of Columbia, with no representatives or senators, is allocated three electoral votes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Both the president and the vice president serve a four-year term, and the president may be reelected to the office only once, for one additional four-year term.[r]

The U.S. federal judiciary, whose judges are all appointed for life by the president with Senate approval, consists primarily of the U.S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Supreme Court, the U.S. courts of appeals, and the U.S. district courts.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The lowest level in the federal judiciary is the federal district court, which decides all cases considered to be under "original jurisdiction", such as federal statutes, constitutional law, or international treaties.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After a federal district court has decided a case, its ruling may be contested and sent to a higher court, a federal court of appeals.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The U.S. judicial system's 12 federal circuits divide the country into 12 separate geographic administrative regions for appeals decisions.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The next and highest court in the system is the Supreme Court of the United States.[249] The U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Supreme Court interprets laws and overturns those it finds unconstitutional.[249] On average, the Supreme Court receives about 7,000 appeals petitions for writs of certiorari each year, but only grants about 80.[250] Consisting of nine members led by the Chief Justice of the United States, the court judges each case before it by majority decision.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In the case of a presidential impeachment trial in the Senate, the chief justice presides. As with all other federal judges, the members are appointed for life by the sitting president with Senate approval when a vacancy becomes available.[251]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>There are about 18,000 U.S. police agencies from local to national level in the United States.[304] Law in the United States is mainly enforced by local police departments and sheriff departments in their municipal or county jurisdictions.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The state police departments have authority in their respective state, and federal agencies such as the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Marshals Service have national jurisdiction and specialized duties, such as protecting civil rights, national security, enforcing U.S. federal courts' rulings and federal laws, and interstate criminal activity.[305] State courts conduct almost all civil and criminal trials,[306] while federal courts adjudicate the much smaller number of civil and criminal cases that relate to federal law.[307]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>On the collegiate level, earnings for the member institutions exceed $1 billion annually,[665] and college football and basketball attract large audiences, as the NCAA March Madness tournament and the College Football Playoff are some of the most watched national sporting events.[666] In the U.S., the intercollegiate sports level serves as the main feeder system for professional and Olympic sports, with significant exceptions such as Minor League Baseball.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This differs greatly from practices in nearly all other countries, where publicly and privately funded sports organizations serve this function.[667]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Brown boarded the train and talked with passengers for over an hour, not concealing his identity. (Because of his abolitionist work in Kansas, Brown was a "notorious" celebrity;[52][53] he was well known to any newspaper reader.) Brown then told the train crew they could continue.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>According to the conductor's telegram they had been detained for five hours,[8]: 5  but according to other sources the conductor did not think it prudent to proceed until sunrise, when it could more easily be verified that no damage had been done to the tracks or bridge, and that no one would shoot at them.[51]: 317 [54][55][56] The passengers were cold on the stopped train, with the engine shut down; normally the temperature would have been around 5 °C (41 °F),[57] but it was "unusually cold".[58]: 8  Brown's men had blankets over their shoulders and arms;[58]: 12  John Cook reported later having been "chilled through".[59]: 12  The passengers were allowed to get off and they "went into the hotel and remained there, in great alarm, for four or five hours".[60]: 175<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Anderson, Osborne P. (1861). <<Q_RELEVANT>>A Voice from Harper's Ferry: A Narrative of Events at Harper's Ferry : with Incidents Prior and Subsequent to Its Capture by Captain Brown and His Men.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Boston.{{cite book}}:  CS1 maint: location missing publisher (link)<</Q_RELEVANT>>

(1861). <<Q_RELEVANT>>A Voice from Harper's Ferry: A Narrative of Events at Harper's Ferry : with Incidents Prior and Subsequent to Its Capture by Captain Brown and His Men.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Boston.{{cite book}}:  CS1 maint: location missing publisher (link)<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>John Brown rented the Kennedy Farmhouse, with a small cabin nearby, 4 miles (6.4 km) north of Harpers Ferry, in Washington County, Maryland,[11] and took up residence under the name Isaac Smith.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Brown came with a small group of men minimally trained for military action. <<Q_RELEVANT>>His group eventually included 21 men besides himself (16 white men, five Black men).<</Q_RELEVANT>> Northern abolitionist groups sent 198 breech-loading .52-caliber Sharps carbines ("Beecher's Bibles"). <<A_RELEVANT>>He ordered from a blacksmith in Connecticut 950 pikes, for use by Black men untrained in the use of firearms, as few were.[12]: 19–20  He told curious neighbors that they were tools for mining, which aroused no suspicion as for years the possibility of local mining for metals had been explored.[13]: 17  Brown "frequently took home with him parcels of earth, which he pretended to analyse in search of minerals.<</A_RELEVANT>> Often his neighbors would visit him when he was making his chemical experiments and so well did he act his part that he was looked upon as one of profound learning and calculated to be a most useful man to the neighborhood."[14]

Many of John Brown's homes are today small museums. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The only major street named for John Brown is in Port-au-Prince, Haiti (where there is also an Avenue Charles Sumner).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In Harpers Ferry today, the engine house, now known as John Brown's Fort, sits in a park, open to walk through, where there is an interpretive display summarizing the events.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Another monument is the cenotaph to three black participants, in Oberlin, Ohio.

<<A_RELEVANT>>As Brown wrote in 1851: "The trial for life of one bold and to some extent successful man, for defending his rights in good earnest, would arouse more sympathy throughout the nation than the accumulated wrongs and suffering of more than three millions of our submissive colored population."[3]: 240  According to his son Salmon, fifty years later: "He wanted to bring on the war.<</A_RELEVANT>> I have heard him talk of it many times."[3]: 238   Brown saw to it that his arrest, trial, and execution received as much publicity as possible. <<Q_RELEVANT>>He "ask[ed] that the incendiary constitution he carried with him be read aloud".[3]: 240  "He seemed very fond of talking."[3]: 240  Authorities deliberately prevented spectators from being close enough to Brown to hear him speak during his short trip to the gallows, but he did give what became his famous final message to a jailer who had asked for his autograph.[3]: 256<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>All save the last were held in the engine house.[66]: 446  According to a newspaper report, there were "not less than sixty"; another report says "upwards of seventy".[58]: 13  They were detained in "a large building further down the yard".[67] The number of rebels sometimes was inflated because some observers, who had to remain at a distance, thought that the hostages were part of Brown's party.[58]: 15<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Wise interviewed Brown while he, along with Stevens, was lying on the floor of the paymaster's office at the Arsenal, where they would remain until, over thirty hours later, they were moved to the Jefferson County jail.[60]: 205  Brown, despite his wounds, was "courteous and afable".[60]: 204  Andrew Hunter took notes,[97]: 167 [60]: 194  but there is no transcript of this interview.<</Q_RELEVANT>> One exchange was as follows:

property_documents.title: Reconstruction era
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Civil War had immense social implications for the United States.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Emancipation had altered the legal status of 3.5 million persons, threatened the end of the plantation economy of the South, and provoked questions regarding the legal and social inequality of the races.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The end of the war was accompanied by a large migration of newly freed people to the cities,[20] where they were relegated to the lowest paying jobs, such as unskilled and service labor. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Men worked as rail workers, rolling and lumber mills workers, and hotel workers.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Black women were largely confined to domestic work employed as cooks, maids, and child nurses, or in hotels and laundries.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The large population of slave artisans during the prewar period did not translate into a large number of free artisans during Reconstruction.[21] The dislocations had a severe negative impact on the Black population, with a large amount of sickness and death.[22]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The Confederate States in 1861 had 297 towns and cities, with a total population of 835,000 people; of these, 162—with 681,000 people—were at some point occupied by Union forces. Eleven cities were destroyed or severely damaged by military action, including Atlanta, Charleston, Columbia, and Richmond, though the rate of damage in smaller towns was much lower.[25] Farms were in disrepair, and the prewar stock of horses, mules, and cattle was much depleted. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Forty percent of Southern livestock had been killed.[26] The South's farms were not highly mechanized, but the value of farm implements and machinery according to the 1860 Census was $81 million and had been reduced 40% by 1870.[27] The transportation infrastructure lay in ruins, with little railroad or riverboat service available to move crops and animals to market.[28] Railroad mileage was located mostly in rural areas; over two-thirds of the South's rails, bridges, rail yards, repair shops, and rolling stock were in areas reached by Union armies, which systematically destroyed what they could.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Even in untouched areas, the lack of maintenance and repair, the absence of new equipment, the heavy over-use, and the deliberate relocation of equipment by the Confederates from remote areas to the war zone ensured the system would be ruined at war's end.[25] Restoring the infrastructure—especially the railroad system—became a high priority for Reconstruction state governments.[29]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Over a quarter of Southern White men of military age—the backbone of the White workforce—died during the war, leaving their families destitute,[26] and per capita income for White Southerners declined from $125 in 1857 to a low of $80 in 1879.<</Q_RELEVANT>> By the end of the 19th century and well into the 20th century, the South was locked into a system of poverty. <<Q_RELEVANT>>How much of this failure was caused by the war and by previous reliance on slavery remains the subject of debate among economists and historians.[30] In both the North and South, modernization and industrialization were the focus of the post-war recovery, built on the growth of cities, railroads, factories, and banks and led by Radical Republicans and former Whigs.[31][32]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Stevens and his followers viewed secession as having left the states in a status like new territories.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Sumner argued that secession had destroyed statehood but the Constitution still extended its authority and its protection over individuals, as in existing U.S. territories.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Republicans sought to prevent Johnson's Southern politicians from "restoring the historical subordination of Negroes".<</Q_RELEVANT>> Since slavery was abolished, the Three-fifths Compromise no longer applied to counting the population of Blacks. After the 1870 Census, the South would gain numerous representatives in Congress, based on the full population of freedmen.[i] One Illinois Republican expressed a common fear that if the South were allowed to simply restore its previous established powers, that the "reward of treason will be an increased representation".[46][47][page needed]

On January 1, 1863, Lincoln issued the final Emancipation Proclamation, naming ten states in which slaves would be "forever free". <<Q_RELEVANT>>The proclamation does not name the states of Tennessee (because it was under Union control) or Kentucky, Missouri, Maryland, and Delaware (because, though slave states, they had not seceded) and specifically excludes numerous counties in some other states.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Eventually, as the U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Army advanced into the Confederacy, millions of slaves were set free. Many of these freedmen joined the U.S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Army, as the Emancipation Proclamation authorized them to do, and fought in battles against the Confederate forces.[73][79][84] Yet hundreds of thousands of freed slaves died during emancipation from illnesses that devastated army regiments.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Freed slaves suffered from smallpox, yellow fever, and malnutrition.[85]

property_documents.title: Dred Scott v. Sandford
property_documents.document:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>Although Chief Justice Taney and several other justices hoped the decision would settle the slavery controversy, which was increasingly dividing the American public, the decision only exacerbated interstate tension.[10] Taney's majority opinion suited the slaveholding states, but was intensely decried in all the other states.[3] The decision inflamed the national debate over slavery and deepened the divide that led ultimately to the American Civil War.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1865, after the Union's victory, the Court's ruling in Dred Scott was superseded by passage of the Thirteenth Amendment to the U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Constitution, which outlawed slavery, and by Congress with the Civil Rights Act of 1866 conferring full citizenship and equal rights flowing from it. <<Q_RELEVANT>>After Southern lawyers and courts countermanded this federal law with state law, Congress and three-quarters of the states in 1868 constitutionalized the 1866 Act by enacting the Fourteenth Amendment, whose first section guaranteed citizenship for "[a]ll persons born or naturalized in the United States and subject to the jurisdiction thereof."<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Reviewing the court's past decisions on freedom suits, Norris acknowledged that if Rachel v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Walker was allowed to stand, his client would lose.[31] Norris then challenged the concept of "once free, always free", and asserted that the court under Tompkins had been wrong to rule that the Ordinance of 1787 remained in force after the ratification of the U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Constitution in 1788.[31] Finally, he argued that the Missouri Compromise should be disregarded whenever it interfered with Missouri law, and that the laws of other states should not be enforced, if their enforcement would cause Missouri citizens to lose their property.[31] In support of his argument, he cited Chief Justice Taney's opinion in the United States Supreme Court case Strader v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Graham, which argued that the status of a slave returning from a free state must be determined by the slave state itself.[31][23]: 63  According to historian Walter Ehrlich, the closing of Norris's brief was "a racist harangue that not only revealed the prejudices of its author, but also indicated how the Dred Scott case had become a vehicle for the expression of such views".[23]: 63  Noting that Norris's proslavery "doctrines" were later incorporated into the court's final decision,[23]: 62  Ehrlich writes (emphasis his):<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Historians agree that the Court decision was a major disaster for the nation as it dramatically inflamed tensions leading to the Civil War.[11][12][13] The ruling is widely considered to have had the intent of bringing finality to the territorial crisis resulting from the Louisiana Purchase by creating a constitutional right to own slaves anywhere in the country, while permanently disenfranchising all people of African descent, in an act generally believed to constitute blatant judicial activism.[14] Often cited in proof of this is the court's decision to go out of its way to overturn the Missouri Compromise, which had already been replaced with the Kansas–Nebraska Act and thus was a legally moot issue, because the latter act was determined by the due process of popular sovereignty, and thus could not be overturned the same way as the Missouri Compromise.[15] During the 1860 United States elections, Republicans rejected the ruling as being corrupted by partisanship and non-binding because the court had no jurisdiction.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Their presidential nominee Abraham Lincoln stated he would not permit slavery anywhere in the country except where it already existed, which directly contradicted the court's ruling.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>His election is considered the final event that led the Southern states to secede from the Union, igniting the Civil War.[16]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Southern Democrats considered Republicans to be lawless rebels who were provoking disunion by their refusal to accept the Supreme Court's decision as the law of the land.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Many northern opponents of slavery offered a legal argument for refusing to acknowledge the Dred Scott decision on the Missouri Compromise.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>They argued, following Justice Curtis' dissenting opinion, that the Court's determination that the federal courts had no jurisdiction to hear the case rendered the remainder of the decision a non-binding obiter dictum—an advisement rather than an authoritative interpretation of the law.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Stephen Douglas attacked that position in the Lincoln–Douglas debates:
