Of the languages of Cyprus, the two official languages are Turkish and Greek. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The most used languages by population are Greek in the south followed by Turkish in the north.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Two minority languages are recognized: Armenian, and Cypriot Maronite Arabic, a hybrid of mostly medieval Arabic vernaculars with strong influence from contact with Turkish and Greek, spoken by approximately 1,000 people.[46]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In The Oxford Handbook of the Archaeology of the Levant: c. 8000–332 BCE (OHAL; 2013), the definition of the Levant for the specific purposes of the book is synonymous to that of the Arabic "bilad al-sham, 'the land of sham [Syria]'", translating in Western parlance to greater Syria.[35] OHAL defines the boundaries of the Levant as follows.[35][5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>As a name for the contemporary region, several dictionaries consider Levant to be archaic.[12][13][14] The noun Levant and adjective Levantine are sometimes used to describe the ancient and modern culture area formerly called Syro-Palestinian.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Archaeologists now speak of the Levant and Levantine archaeology,[15][16][17] food scholars of Levantine cuisine, and Latin Catholics of the Levant are sometimes called Levantines,[18] though the term is normally used to describe the Levant population more widely.[19][20][21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Today, "Levant" is the term typically used by archaeologists and historians with reference to the history of the region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Scholars have adopted the term Levant to identify the region due to its being a "wider, yet relevant, cultural corpus" that does not have the "political overtones" of Syria-Palestine.[d][e] The term is also used for modern events, peoples, states or parts of states in the same region, namely Cyprus, Egypt, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria, and Turkey are sometimes considered Levant countries (compare with Near East, Middle East, Eastern Mediterranean and West Asia).[citation needed] Several researchers include the island of Cyprus in Levantine studies, including the Council for British Research in the Levant (CBRL),[27] the UCLA Near Eastern Languages and Cultures department,[28] Journal of Levantine Studies[29] and the UCL Institute of Archaeology,[8] the last of which has dated the connection between Cyprus and mainland Levant to the early Iron Age.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Archaeologists seeking a neutral orientation that is neither biblical nor national have used terms such as Levantine archaeology and archaeology of the Southern Levant.[30][31]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Levant[b] is a subregion of West Asia along the Eastern Mediterranean that forms part of the Middle East.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The term is often used in conjunction with historical or cultural references.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In its narrowest sense, used in archaeology and other contexts, the Levant refers to Cyprus and land bordering the Levantine Sea (Mediterranean) in West Asia[4][5] that includes Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine, Israel, and south Cilicia (Turkey).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In its widest historical sense, the Levant included all the Eastern Mediterranean;[6] extending from Greece to Egypt and Cyrenaica (Eastern Libya).[3][7] The Levantine corridor represents the land bridge between Africa and Eurasia,[5] has been described as the crossroads of West Asia, Eastern Mediterranean, and Northeast Africa,[8] and geologically as the "northwest of the Arabian plate".[9]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In the 13th and 14th centuries, levante was used for Italian maritime commerce in the Eastern Mediterranean, including Greece, Anatolia, Syria-Palestine, and Egypt, that is the lands east of Venice.[3] It derives from the Italian levante, meaning "rising", implying the rising of the Sun in the east, and is broadly equivalent to the Mashriq,[c][10] meaning "eastern place, where the Sun rises".[11] Eventually the term was restricted to the Muslim countries of Syria-Palestine and Egypt.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The term entered English in the 15th century from French.[6] In 1581, England set up the Levant Company to trade with the Ottoman Empire.[3] The name Levant States was used to refer to the French mandate over Syria and Lebanon after World War I, so Levant has come to refer to modern Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, Israel, Jordan, and Cyprus.[3]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: The organization that owned the iron‑clad warship *Nemesis* (built by Cammell Laird in the United Kingdom) also supplied indigo dye (a blue pigment), cultivated cotton from both *Gossypium barbadense* and *Gossypium hirsutum*, and traded tea that was prepared by steeping. Based on the official inception and dissolution dates of this entity, how many decades did it exist?

entity_document.title: East India Company
entity_document.text:
In the 18th Century, the primary source of the Company's profits in Bengal became taxation in conquered and controlled provinces, as the factories became fortresses and administrative hubs for networks of tax collectors that expanded into enormous cities. <<A_RELEVANT>>The Mughal Empire was the richest in the world in 1700, and the East India Company tried to strip it bare for a century thereafter.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Dalrymple calls it "the single largest transfer of wealth until the Nazis."[45] What was in the 17th century the production capital of the world for textiles was forced to become a market for British-made textiles.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Statues, jewels, and various other valuables were moved from the palaces of Bengal to the townhouses of the English countryside.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Bengal in particular suffered the worst of Company tax farming, highlighted by the Great Bengal famine of 1770.[45]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In September the company took out a loan from the Bank of England, to be repaid from the sale of goods later that month.<</Q_RELEVANT>> But with buyers scarce, most of the sale had to be postponed, and when the loan fell due, the company's coffers were empty. <<Q_RELEVANT>>On October 29 the bank refused to renew the loan.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>That decision set in motion a chain of events that made the American Revolution inevitable.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The East India Company had eighteen million pounds of tea sitting in British warehouses.<</A_RELEVANT>> A huge amount of tea as assets which were lying unsold. Selling it in a hurry would do wonders for its finances.[89]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The company's headquarters in London, from which much of India was governed, was East India House in Leadenhall Street.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After occupying premises in Philpot Lane from 1600 to 1621; in Crosby House, Bishopsgate from 1621 to 1638; and in Leadenhall Street from 1638 to 1648, the company moved into Craven House, an Elizabethan mansion in Leadenhall Street.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The building had become known as East India House by 1661. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It was completely rebuilt and enlarged in 1726–1729 and further significantly remodelled and expanded in 1796–1800.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It was finally vacated in 1860 and demolished in 1861–1862.[95] The site is now occupied by the Lloyd's building.[96]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The first century of the Company, despite its original profits coming primarily from piracy in the Spice Islands between competing European powers and their companies,[45] saw the East India Company change focus after suffering a major setback in 1623 when their factory in Amboyna in the Moluccas was attacked by the Dutch.<</QA_RELEVANT>> This compelled the company to formally abandon their efforts in the Spice Islands, and turn their attention to Bengal where, by this time, they were making steady, if less exciting, profits.[45] After gaining the indifferent patronage of the Mughal Empire, whose cities were "the megacities of their time" and whose wealth was unrivalled outside of Asia in the 17th century,[45] the Company's first century in the Mughal-ruled areas was spent cultivating their relationship with the Mughal Dynasty, and conducting peaceful trade at great profit. <<Q_RELEVANT>>At first it should be said the EIC was drawn into the Mughal system, acting as a kind of vassal to Mughal authority in present-day Bangladesh: it was from this position that the Company would ultimately outplay and outmanoeuvre all competing powers in the region, to eventually use that very system to hold power itself.[45]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The company started selling opium to Chinese merchants in the 1770s in exchange for goods like porcelain and tea,[67] causing a series of opioid addiction outbreaks across China in 1820.[68] The ruling Qing dynasty outlawed the opium trade in 1796 and 1800,[69] but British merchants continued illegally nonetheless.[70][71] The Qing took measures to prevent the East India Company from selling opium, and destroyed tens of thousands of chests of opium already in the country.[72] This series of events led to the First Opium War in 1839, which involved a succession of British naval attacks along the Chinese coast over the course of several months.<</QA_RELEVANT>> As part of the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842, the Qing were forced to give British merchants special treatment and the right to sell opium. The Chinese also ceded territory to the British, including the island of Hong Kong.[73]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The East India Company had also been granted competitive advantages over colonial American tea importers to sell tea from its colonies in Asia in American colonies.<</QA_RELEVANT>> This led to the Boston Tea Party of 1773 in which protesters boarded British ships and threw the tea overboard. <<Q_RELEVANT>>When protesters successfully prevented the unloading of tea in three other colonies and in Boston, Governor Thomas Hutchinson of the Province of Massachusetts Bay refused to allow the tea to be returned to Britain.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This was one of the incidents which led to the American Revolution and independence of the American colonies.[92]

property_documents.title: Cammell Laird
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Between 1829 and 1947, over 1,100 vessels of all kinds were launched from the Cammell Laird slipways into the River Mersey.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Among the many famous ships made by the companies were the world's first steel ship, the Ma Roberts, built in 1858 for Dr.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Livingstone's Zambezi expedition, CSS Alabama that was built in 1862 for the Confederate States of America, HMS Caroline that holds the record fastest build time of any significant warship (nine months from her keel being laid till her launch), the first all-welded ship, the Fullagar built in 1920, Cunard's second RMS Mauretania, the aircraft carrier HMS Ark Royal (1937) the battleship HMS Prince of Wales (1941) and the largest vessel to have been built for the Royal Navy up to that time, HMS Ark Royal (1950).<</Q_RELEVANT>>

In 1903 the businesses of Messrs. Cammell and Laird merged to create a company at the forefront of shipbuilding.[3] The company also built a number of vehicles for the London Underground. An order was placed for 20 trailer cars and 20 control trailer cars in 1919, which were known as 1920 Stock, and were the first tube cars to be built with doors operated by compressed air. <<Q_RELEVANT>>They ran with converted French motor cars, originally built in 1906.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The doors were fitted with a sensitive edge, designed to re-open the door if someone became trapped in it, but the mechanism was too sensitive, and was removed after an initial trial period.[4] The cars continued in operation until 1938, eight years after the motor cars were withdrawn, but following withdrawal, five cars became a mobile training school.[5] Cammell Laird also built a number of Standard Stock vehicles for the Underground.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>They were one of five builders approached to build a sample car to a general specification, which were put into service in February 1923, and three of the builders subsequently built production runs.[6] The company supplied 41 motor cars and 40 trailer cars in 1923, 25 control trailers in 1924, and a further 48 motor cars in 1925.[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Johnson, Cammell & Co., later Charles Cammell & Co., was founded by Charles Cammell and Henry and Thomas Johnson: it made, amongst many other metal products, iron wheels and rails for Britain's railways and was based in Sheffield.[3]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Cammell Laird is a British shipbuilding company.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It was formed from the merger of Laird Brothers of Birkenhead and Johnson Cammell & Co of Sheffield at the turn of the twentieth century.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The company also built railway rolling stock until 1929, when that side of the business was separated and became part of the Metropolitan-Cammell Carriage & Wagon Company.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1898, Cammell provided the half-inch armour plate used to fabricate the four Fowler Armoured Road Trains built during the Second Anglo-Boer War.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The armoured road train was the first self-propelled, free-roaming, armoured military land vehicle ever built, predating the tanks of World War One by nearly two decades.<</A_RELEVANT>>

Part of the shipyard site was leased by the Coastline Group as a ship repair facility. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Coastline eventually bought part of the shipyard and adopted the Cammell Laird name, before floating on the London stock exchange in 1997 and acquiring dockyards at Teesside, Tyneside and Gibraltar.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>After experiencing financial difficulties, partly due to the late withdrawal from a £50 million refit contract for the cruise ship Costa Classica cruise ship by Costa Crociere, the company was forced to enter receivership in April 2001, and the Birkenhead, Teesside and Tyneside shipyards owned by Cammell Laird shiprepair were acquired by the A&P Shiprepair Group in 2001.[10] Cammell Laird Gibraltar, the Royal Dockyard facility in Gibraltar, was disposed of through a local management buyout.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2007, it was announced that the occupiers of Cammell Laird Dock, Northwestern Shiprepairers & Shipbuilders, had acquired the rights to the Cammell Laird name.[13] On 17 November 2008, Northwestern Shiprepairers & Shipbuilders officially renamed itself Cammell Laird Shiprepairers & Shipbuilders Limited, stating that recent economic success had made the time right, and that "Cammell Laird is an internationally recognised brand which carries tremendous goodwill when bidding for contracts."[13][14]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The yard was named as part of a consortium to build the Royal Navy's new Type 26 Frigate in September 2023.[26] BAE Systems are the primary contractor, but Cammell Laird will be used to build sections of HMS Birmingham.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The Laird Company was founded by William Laird, who had established the Birkenhead Iron Works in 1824. When he was joined by his son, John Laird in 1828, their first ship was an iron barge.[1] John realised that the techniques of making boilers could be applied to making ships. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The company soon became pre-eminent in the manufacture of iron ships and also made major advances in propulsion.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In 1860, John Laird was joined in the business by his three sons, renaming the company John Laird, Sons & Co. The sons continued the business after their father's death in 1874 as Laird Brothers.[2]

property_documents.title: Gossypium hirsutum
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Gossypium hirsutum, also known as upland cotton or Mexican cotton, is the most widely planted species of cotton in the world.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Globally, about 90% of all cotton production is of cultivars derived from this species.[2] In the United States, the world's largest exporter of cotton, it constitutes approximately 95% of all cotton production.[3][4] It is native from Mexico to Ecuador and northeast Brazil, the Leeward Antilles in the Caribbean and the Pacific (Fiji, Marianas, Polynesia and Revillagigedo Islands).[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Zuni people use this plant to make ceremonial garments,[8] and the fuzz is made into cords and used ceremonially.[9]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Gossypium hirsutum includes a number of varieties or cross-bred cultivars with varying fiber lengths and tolerances to a number of growing conditions.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The longer length varieties are called "long staple upland" and the shorter length varieties are referred to as "short staple upland". <<Q_RELEVANT>>The long staple varieties are the most widely cultivated in commercial production.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Besides being fibre crops, Gossypium hirsutum and Gossypium herbaceum are the main species used to produce cottonseed oil.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Archeological evidence from the Tehuacan Valley in Mexico shows the cultivation of this species as long ago as 3,500 BC, although there is as yet no evidence as to exactly where it may have been first domesticated.[7] This is the earliest evidence of cotton cultivation in the Americas found thus far.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>This species shows extrafloral nectar production.[10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>It is believed that Gossypium hirsutum was created when wild Mexican cotton breeds mixed with Gossypium herbaceum around 5-10 million years ago, producing  a hybrid species with 26 pairs of chromosomes via polyploidy.[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Gossypium barbadense var. marie-galante (G.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Watt) A. Chev., Rev. Int. Bot. Appl Agric. Trop. 18:118. 1938.

One possible explanation was that the changes happened accidentally in a region with long growing season and then were introduced to the Sea Islands. In the 1960s and 1970s, S. G. Stephens performed an experiment where he hybridized a G. barbadense with short coarse fibers and long growing season with a wild form of G. hirsutum that had the same short fiber and long growing season, but the fibers were fine. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It seemed reasonable the resulting plant produced fine fibers, but was surprised to find it also had long fiber and short growing season.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He then demonstrated this could be rather easily back-hybridized (see introgression) to form a cotton that retained these desirable characteristics, yet was almost entirely G. barbadense.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He  argued that such an event could have happened accidentally in the 18th century, resulting in the long, fine fiber G. barbadense of today.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, since this event could not have happened in the Sea Islands, it is not sufficient to explain the Sea Islands' distinctive product.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Most G. barbadense production comes from cultivars that produce particularly long fiber, and most of that is made into clothing.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Fine (thin) yarn requires long fiber. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In turn, this thin yarn is required for intermediate products like lace and high thread-count cloth.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The long-fiber cultivars also tend to have particularly strong fibers, making them useful for various industrial products.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Historically, G. barbadense has been used for the cords of automobile tires and cloth for aircraft wings.[2]: 85  It is also used for sewing machine thread.[2]: 277<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Some growers have established trademarks for yarn or finished items made of G. barbadense fiber.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Caribbean producers banded together in 1933 to form the West Indian Sea Island Cotton Association. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The organization allows makers of yarn and finished goods to use the “WISICA” trademark, provided the items are made from Sea Island of the Caribbean cotton and meet certain quality requirements. [18][21] Likewise, a group of southwestern United States growers established the trademark Supima for products made of American Pima fiber.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The origins of Sea Island cotton has been the subject of considerable controversy.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Nevertheless, developing the market class required developing cultivars that would be productive in the Sea Islands, and developing a product that was distinct from other kinds of cotton.[2]: 89  It also required at least some producers and consumers to agree "Sea Island" was a useful category.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Sea island never fully recovered from the disruptions of the U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Civil War.[2]: 136  In the early 20th century, the boll weevil caused tremendous damage in the traditional cotton-growing regions of the United States.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Sea Island cultivars were particularly susceptible. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Also, wet conditions on the islands moderated soil temperatures, further favoring the insect.[2]: 291–292  Production of Sea Island on a commercial scale ended in 1920.[2]: 332<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The development of the market class started in 1820, when Jumel's cotton entered commercial production.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This was a type of cotton that had been growing in the region for some time, but a French engineer named Jumel recognized its potential as a source of fiber when he saw it growing as an ornamental in a garden in Cairo. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Based on its description, it seems likely it was the recently developed long fiber kind of G. barbadense from the New World.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Encouraged by the success of Jumel's cotton, Egyptians tested other seeds, including Sea Island. The next major cultivar in Egypt, "early Ashmouni," likely was a hybrid between Jumel and a Sea Island cultivar. Likewise, the following major cultivar, "Mit Afifi," likely was a hybrid between early Ashmouni and a Sea Island cultivar. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Many more cultivars followed.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Pima is a name often used for cotton grown in the Southwestern United States.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This market class consists of extra-long G. barbadense. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It was originally known as "American Egyptian", but eventually the name "Pima" became more popular.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Since the name "Pima" also has been applied to extra-long staple cotton growing in countries such as Peru, Australia, and Israel,[13] sometimes the name "American Pima" is used to clarify the origin.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The name "American Pima" was formally adopted by the United States government in 1970.[14]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The market class “Sea Island of the Caribbean” developed from efforts to revitalize cotton production in the Caribbean region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It never became a major crop for the region, nevertheless the market class is significant for the luxury market.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>One example is the steeping of corn (or maize), part of the milling process.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As described by the US Corn Refiners Association, harvested kernels of corn are cleaned and then steeped in water at a temperature of 50 °C (120 °F) for 30 to 40 hours.[1] In the process their moisture content rises from 15% to 45% and their volume more than doubles.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The gluten bonds in the corn are weakened and starch is released. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The corn is then ground to break free the germ and other components, and the water used (steepwater), which has absorbed various nutrients, is recycled for use in animal feeds.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Dried teas as loose tea or tea bags are prepared for drinking by steeping the leaves in just boiled or heated water to release the flavour and nutrients in the dried tea into the water.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This is often done in a cup, mug, teapot, pitcher or urn. <<Q_RELEVANT>>A tea infuser or a tea strainer may be used to assist in this process.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>There is a huge variety of teas available in the market with broad based categories like oolong, green, black, white etc. and other specialized ones catering to particular regions such as Assam, Darjeeling [2] etc.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Each tea has to be prepared properly pertaining to their make and quality.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Steeping is the soaking of an organic solid, such as leaves, in a liquid (usually water) to extract flavours or to soften it.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The specific process of teas being prepared for drinking by leaving the leaves in heated water to release the flavour and nutrients is known as steeping.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Herbal teas may be prepared by decoction, infusion, or maceration. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some solids are soaked to remove an ingredient, such as salt, where the solute is not the desired product.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Steeping grain is a part of making beer.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In September the company took out a loan from the Bank of England, to be repaid from the sale of goods later that month.<</Q_RELEVANT>> But with buyers scarce, most of the sale had to be postponed, and when the loan fell due, the company's coffers were empty. <<Q_RELEVANT>>On October 29 the bank refused to renew the loan.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>That decision set in motion a chain of events that made the American Revolution inevitable.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The East India Company had eighteen million pounds of tea sitting in British warehouses.<</A_RELEVANT>> A huge amount of tea as assets which were lying unsold. Selling it in a hurry would do wonders for its finances.[89]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The company's headquarters in London, from which much of India was governed, was East India House in Leadenhall Street.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After occupying premises in Philpot Lane from 1600 to 1621; in Crosby House, Bishopsgate from 1621 to 1638; and in Leadenhall Street from 1638 to 1648, the company moved into Craven House, an Elizabethan mansion in Leadenhall Street.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The building had become known as East India House by 1661. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It was completely rebuilt and enlarged in 1726–1729 and further significantly remodelled and expanded in 1796–1800.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It was finally vacated in 1860 and demolished in 1861–1862.[95] The site is now occupied by the Lloyd's building.[96]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The first century of the Company, despite its original profits coming primarily from piracy in the Spice Islands between competing European powers and their companies,[45] saw the East India Company change focus after suffering a major setback in 1623 when their factory in Amboyna in the Moluccas was attacked by the Dutch.<</QA_RELEVANT>> This compelled the company to formally abandon their efforts in the Spice Islands, and turn their attention to Bengal where, by this time, they were making steady, if less exciting, profits.[45] After gaining the indifferent patronage of the Mughal Empire, whose cities were "the megacities of their time" and whose wealth was unrivalled outside of Asia in the 17th century,[45] the Company's first century in the Mughal-ruled areas was spent cultivating their relationship with the Mughal Dynasty, and conducting peaceful trade at great profit. <<Q_RELEVANT>>At first it should be said the EIC was drawn into the Mughal system, acting as a kind of vassal to Mughal authority in present-day Bangladesh: it was from this position that the Company would ultimately outplay and outmanoeuvre all competing powers in the region, to eventually use that very system to hold power itself.[45]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The company started selling opium to Chinese merchants in the 1770s in exchange for goods like porcelain and tea,[67] causing a series of opioid addiction outbreaks across China in 1820.[68] The ruling Qing dynasty outlawed the opium trade in 1796 and 1800,[69] but British merchants continued illegally nonetheless.[70][71] The Qing took measures to prevent the East India Company from selling opium, and destroyed tens of thousands of chests of opium already in the country.[72] This series of events led to the First Opium War in 1839, which involved a succession of British naval attacks along the Chinese coast over the course of several months.<</QA_RELEVANT>> As part of the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842, the Qing were forced to give British merchants special treatment and the right to sell opium. The Chinese also ceded territory to the British, including the island of Hong Kong.[73]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The East India Company had also been granted competitive advantages over colonial American tea importers to sell tea from its colonies in Asia in American colonies.<</QA_RELEVANT>> This led to the Boston Tea Party of 1773 in which protesters boarded British ships and threw the tea overboard. <<Q_RELEVANT>>When protesters successfully prevented the unloading of tea in three other colonies and in Boston, Governor Thomas Hutchinson of the Province of Massachusetts Bay refused to allow the tea to be returned to Britain.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This was one of the incidents which led to the American Revolution and independence of the American colonies.[92]
property_documents.paragraph: In the 18th Century, the primary source of the Company's profits in Bengal became taxation in conquered and controlled provinces, as the factories became fortresses and administrative hubs for networks of tax collectors that expanded into enormous cities. <<A_RELEVANT>>The Mughal Empire was the richest in the world in 1700, and the East India Company tried to strip it bare for a century thereafter
